name: Guillotine System
description: Build guillotine choke threats from front headlock, guard, and scrambles — prioritizing angle, wrist depth, and neck safety over brute force.
shortInstruction: Deep wrist, elbow tight, cut the angle, squeeze — the guillotine is a position, not just a grip.
summary: The guillotine is the most accessible front headlock choke and the first choke most BJJ practitioners learn. The system includes multiple variations: the standard arm-in guillotine (from guard), the arm-out guillotine (from front headlock), the high-wrist guillotine (for deeper neck penetration), and the Marcelotine (Marcelo Garcia's no-gi variation). The key principle across all variations is that the guillotine is a position — you must control their posture and create the angle before squeezing.
whyItWorks: The guillotine attacks the neck from the front, where most opponents' head and posture create a natural entry for the choke.
It is available from almost every position: front headlock, guard, scrambles, and failed takedowns.
The arm-in variation (from guard) prevents them from posturing and makes the choke tighter.
Danaher principle: the guillotine is a 'position first, submission second' choke — control their posture, then attack.
commonMistakes: Squeezing before controlling their posture — a postured opponent can relieve the pressure by standing.
Letting the choking arm slide shallow on the neck — a deep wrist is essential for the finish.
Using only arm strength to finish — the finish comes from cutting an angle and using your chest.
Letting them stack you or drive forward — maintain hip distance to keep the angle.
coachingCues: Deep wrist, tight elbow, sharp angle, squeeze.
If you can see their back, your angle is wrong — cut the angle more.
Arm-in is control, arm-out is speed — choose wisely.
The guillotine is a fight for posture — win the posture, win the choke.
safetySummary: The guillotine compresses the neck — apply gradually and release on tap.
Do not crank the opponent's head forward — a clean guillotine is a blood choke, not a neck crank.
Tap early if you feel pressure on your cervical spine — some guillotine variations can cause neck injury.
keyCorrections: If you can't finish, your angle is too square — step to the side and cut the angle.
If they posture out, you lost hip distance — release and reset rather than chasing the choke.
If your wrist is shallow, re-grip deeper — the choking arm must be as deep as possible on the neck.

systemLogic.corePrinciple: Front headlock or guard: secure guillotine grip (deep wrist, elbow tight) → cut the angle (step to the side) → squeeze with chest and arms.

decisionTree.action: pull their head down with legs → cut the angle → finish.
circle to the side → drop weight → finish.
transition to D'Arce or anaconda — the three form a front headlock chain.

moneyDetails: The choking arm must be deep — your wrist should touch their cervical spine, not just the side of their neck.
Your elbow must be tight to your body — a flared elbow gives them the space to posture.
Cut the angle by stepping to the side of their head — a 45-degree angle is ideal.
Squeeze with your chest and shoulder, not just your arms — chest pressure creates a tighter choke.
nextStep: After the guillotine system, learn the high-wrist guillotine and Marcelotine variations.
fixItFast: Wrist is too shallow? Slide deeper — the wrist should be at their spine, not the skin.
They keep posturing? Step further to the side — the angle breaks their posture.
Arm burning out? Use your chest to squeeze — arm-only guillotines burn out fast.
